2026 Paris Motor Show • Citroen 2 CV Fourgonnette Would Get Thumbs up Everywhere, No Greenlight for Production Yet
Half of US-Market BMW M2 Coupe Buyers Want a Manual Whose Future Remains Uncertain
6 photos
Photo: BMW
The M division faces a few problems that enthusiasm alone won't fix. As it happens, the current BMW manual transmission for S58-powered vehicles can't handle the full torque of the twin-turbo I6 engine. According to M boss Frank van Meel, the pool of companies that are capable of supplying manuals for said applications continues to shrink as well.
The problem is compounded by the move toward 48-volt electrification, adding yet another complication that makes the row-your-own transmission's future all the more uncertain. At its core, a transmission is more than merely a collection of gears that BMW and its designated supplier can redesign whenever an engine gains additional torque over the current iteration.
Said transmission, specifically the ZF S6-53 in the M divisions' case, needs a supplier that is willing to develop, validate, and manufacture the unit. From the automaker's standpoint, enough production volume justifies the expense. As manual-equipped performance cars become a smaller part of the market, said business case gets increasingly harder to defend.
A stronger three-pedal tranny could address the S58's torque limitation, but would not solve the 48-volt compatibility issue van Meel acknowledged to BMWBlog. According to van Meel, the company hasn't abandoned the idea of a manual for upcoming S58-powered models. Asked whether the ZF-supplied manual was permanently off the table, van Meel confirmed that M is still looking for solutions.
He declined to offer a guarantee, though, and the awkward part is that M2, M3, and M4 buyers in the US continue to make a case for keeping it alive. Frank van Meel explained that roughly half of G87-generation M2 Coupe vehicles moved in the US market have a manual, representing a substantial share for an option that many automakers have already removed from their performance lineups.
Photo: BMW The limited-edition M3 CS Handschalter offers another indication of demand, for the rear-drive sedan is exclusively manual and exclusively North American for model year 2027. Naturally, the volume split between the US and Canada is heavily weighted toward the former due to dealer footprint and the larger pool of potential customers. Only 40 units are heading to Canada.
BMW sold every single M3 CS Handschalter there will be in roughly a week, and chances are those customers have ponied up top dollar to secure what could possibly be the automaker's final M3 with a manual transmission. Even if it were not, this kind of demand shows that a scarce manual sedan can attract buyers willing to pay well nearly $110,000 like it's no big deal.
The M3 CS Handschalter further exposes a big difference between selling a special-edition manual sedan and sustaining a transmission program across three model lines. BMW can build a limited run using an existing gearbox, targeting customers who specifically want that configuration. Developing a new unit for several future models requires a different level of investment and attention to detail. Simple as that.
BMW and the M division both know the manual remains an emotional selling point, one that differentiates S58-powered vehicles clearly from two-pedal rivals with AMG and RS badging. Even so, van Meel could not promise that the manual would remain available.
Making the manual work together with a 48-volt system is especially difficult, but not impossible. Hyundai and Kia offer such transmissions in Europe, and the key to making it all work is the clutch-by-wire design . The South Korean way includes a third pedal that does not use a mechanical linkage for connecting the clutch. Instead, a sensor on the pedal and an electronic control unit work together with an electromechanical actuator.
